title: Book 6, Chapter 18 — Seventeenth Year of the War—The Sicilian Campaign—Affair of the Hermae—Departure of the Expedition
paragraphs: The same winter the Athenians resolved to sail to Sicily again, this time with a greater armament than the one under Laches and Eurymedon, and to conquer the island if they could. Most of them did not know how large it was, or how many inhabitants it had, Hellenic and barbarian. They did not know either that they were taking on a war little inferior to the one against the Peloponnesians. A merchant ship needs nearly eight days to sail around Sicily, and yet, large as the island is, only two miles of sea keep it from being part of the mainland.

Its settlement came about as follows, and these are the peoples who occupied it. The earliest inhabitants mentioned anywhere in the country are the Cyclopes and Laestrygones. I cannot say what race they were, where they came from or where they went, and I leave my readers with what the poets have said of them and with what is generally known. The Sicanians appear to have come next, although they claim to have been the first of all and to be natives of the soil. The facts show that they were Iberians, driven by the Ligurians from the river Sicanus in Iberia. The island had been called Trinacria, and it took the name Sicania from them; to the present day they inhabit the west of Sicily. When Ilium fell, some of the Trojans escaped from the Achaeans and came in ships to Sicily. They settled next to the Sicanians under the general name of Elymi, and their towns were called Eryx and Egesta. Some of the Phocians settled with them, carried by a storm on their way from Troy, first to Libya and then from there to Sicily. The Sicels crossed over to Sicily from Italy, their first home, fleeing from the Opicans. As tradition says, and as seems not unlikely, they crossed on rafts, having waited until the wind blew down the strait; but perhaps they sailed over in some other way. There are still Sicels in Italy even today, and the country took its name of Italy from Italus, a king of the Sicels who bore that name. These Sicels went to Sicily with a great host, defeated the Sicanians in battle and forced them to move to the south and west of the island. So the island came to be called Sicily instead of Sicania, and the Sicels, once across, enjoyed the richest parts of the country for nearly three hundred years before any Hellenes came to Sicily. Indeed they still hold the center and north of the island. There were also Phoenicians living all around Sicily, who had occupied promontories on the coast and the small islands nearby in order to trade with the Sicels. But when the Hellenes began to arrive by sea in considerable numbers, the Phoenicians abandoned most of their stations. They drew together and made their home at Motye, Soloeis and Panormus, near the Elymi, partly because they trusted in the Elymi’s alliance, and partly because these are the nearest points on the voyage between Carthage and Sicily.

These were the barbarians in Sicily, and this is how they were settled. Of the Hellenes, the first to arrive were Chalcidians from Euboea, with Thucles as their founder. They founded Naxos and built the altar to Apollo Archegetes, which now stands outside the town; the deputies for the games sacrifice on it before sailing from Sicily. Syracuse was founded the year after by Archias, one of the Heraclids from Corinth. He began by driving the Sicels out of the island on which the inner city now stands, although it is no longer surrounded by water. In time the outer town was also taken within the walls and became populous. Meanwhile, in the fifth year after the foundation of Syracuse, Thucles and the Chalcidians set out from Naxos and drove out the Sicels by force of arms. They founded Leontini and afterwards Catana, the Catanians themselves choosing Evarchus as their founder.

About the same time Lamis arrived in Sicily with a colony from Megara. He founded a place called Trotilus beyond the river Pantacyas, then left it and for a short while joined the Chalcidians at Leontini. They drove him out, and he founded Thapsus. After his death his companions were driven out of Thapsus and founded a place called the Hyblaean Megara, Hyblon, a Sicel king, having given up the place and invited them there. They lived here two hundred and forty-five years, and were then expelled from the city and the country by the Syracusan tyrant Gelo. A hundred years after they had settled there, however, and before their expulsion, they sent out Pamillus and founded Selinus; he came from their mother country Megara to join them in founding it. Gela was founded by Antiphemus from Rhodes and Entimus from Crete, who led the colony there together, in the forty-fifth year after the foundation of Syracuse. The town took its name from the river Gelas, and the place where the citadel now stands, which was the first part fortified, is called Lindii. The institutions they adopted were Dorian. About a hundred and eight years after the foundation of Gela, the Geloans founded Acragas (Agrigentum), named after the river of that name, and made Aristonous and Pystilus its founders, giving the colony their own institutions. Zancle was originally founded by pirates from Cuma, the Chalcidian town in the country of the Opicans. Afterwards large numbers came from Chalcis and the rest of Euboea and helped to people the place, its founders being Perieres from Cuma and Crataemenes from Chalcis. The Sicels first gave it the name Zancle, because the place is shaped like a sickle, which the Sicels call zanclon. Later the original settlers were expelled by some Samians and other Ionians, who had landed in Sicily in flight from the Medes, and not long afterwards the Samians were in turn expelled by Anaxilas, tyrant of Rhegium. He colonized the town with a mixed population and changed its name to Messina, after his old country.

Himera was founded from Zancle by Euclides, Simus and Sacon. Most of those who went to the colony were Chalcidians, though they were joined by some exiles from Syracuse, called the Myletidae, who had been defeated in a civil war. The language was a mixture of Chalcidian and Doric, but the institutions that prevailed were Chalcidian. Acrae and Casmenae were founded by the Syracusans: Acrae seventy years after Syracuse, and Casmenae nearly twenty years after Acrae. Camarina was first founded by the Syracusans, close upon a hundred and thirty-five years after the building of Syracuse, with Daxon and Menecolus as its founders. But the Syracusans expelled the Camarinaeans by force of arms for having revolted. Some time later Hippocrates, tyrant of Gela, received their land as a ransom for some Syracusan prisoners and resettled Camarina, acting as its founder himself. Lastly, it was depopulated again by Gelo, and settled for the third time by the Geloans.

Such is the list of the peoples, Hellenic and barbarian, who inhabit Sicily, and such was the size of the island that the Athenians were now bent on invading. In real truth they were ambitious to conquer the whole of it, although they also had the specious aim of helping their kindred and other allies there. But they were especially spurred on by envoys from Egesta, who had come to Athens and begged for their aid more urgently than ever. The Egestaeans had gone to war with their neighbors the Selinuntines over questions of marriage and disputed territory. The Selinuntines had won the alliance of the Syracusans, and were pressing Egesta hard by land and sea. The Egestaeans now reminded the Athenians of the alliance made in the time of Laches, during the former Leontine war, and begged them to send a fleet to their aid. Among a number of other considerations, they urged as a capital argument this one: if the Syracusans were allowed to go unpunished for depopulating Leontini, to ruin the allies Athens still had in Sicily and to gather the whole power of the island into their hands, there would be a danger that one day they would come with a large force, as Dorians to help their Dorian brethren, and as colonists to help the Peloponnesians who had sent them out, and would join these in pulling down the Athenian empire. The Athenians would therefore do well to unite with the allies still left to them and make a stand against the Syracusans, especially as the Egestaeans were prepared to furnish money sufficient for the war. The Athenians heard these arguments repeated constantly in their assemblies by the Egestaeans and their supporters. They voted first to send envoys to Egesta, to see whether the money they talked of was really in the treasury and the temples, and at the same time to find out how the war with the Selinuntines stood.

The Athenian envoys were accordingly dispatched to Sicily. The same winter the Lacedaemonians and their allies, except the Corinthians, marched into the Argive territory. They ravaged a small part of the land, took some yokes of oxen and carried off some grain. They also settled the Argive exiles at Orneae, leaving them a few soldiers taken from the rest of the army. Then they made a truce for a certain time, under which neither the Orneatae nor the Argives were to harm each other’s territory, and returned home with the army. Not long afterwards the Athenians came with thirty ships and six hundred heavy infantry. The Argives joined them with all their forces, marched out and besieged the men in Orneae for one day; but the garrison escaped by night, the besiegers having camped some way off. The next day the Argives discovered this, razed Orneae to the ground and went back again, after which the Athenians went home in their ships. Meanwhile the Athenians carried some of their own cavalry, together with the Macedonian exiles who were at Athens, by sea to Methone on the Macedonian border, and plundered the country of Perdiccas. In response the Lacedaemonians sent to the Thracian Chalcidians, who had a truce with Athens renewed every ten days, and urged them to join Perdiccas in the war; they refused. And the winter ended, and with it the sixteenth year of this war of which Thucydides is the historian.

Early in the spring of the following summer the Athenian envoys arrived from Sicily, and the Egestaeans came with them. They brought sixty talents of uncoined silver as a month’s pay for sixty ships, which they were to ask the Athenians to send. The Athenians held an assembly. They heard the Egestaeans and their own envoys report on the state of affairs generally, and in particular on the money, of which, it was said, there was plenty in the temples and the treasury. The report was as attractive as it was untrue. The Athenians voted to send sixty ships to Sicily under the command of Alcibiades, son of Clinias, Nicias, son of Niceratus, and Lamachus, son of Xenophanes, who were appointed with full powers. They were to help the Egestaeans against the Selinuntines, to restore Leontini if they gained any advantage in the war, and to settle all other matters in Sicily as they judged best for the interests of Athens. Five days later a second assembly was held, to consider the quickest means of equipping the ships and to vote whatever else the generals might need for the expedition. Nicias had been chosen to the command against his will. He thought the state was ill advised, and that on a slight and specious pretext it was aspiring to the conquest of the whole of Sicily, a great matter to achieve. He came forward in the hope of turning the Athenians from the enterprise, and gave them the following counsel:

“This assembly was convened to consider the preparations for sailing to Sicily. Nevertheless I think we still have this question to examine: whether it is better to send out the ships at all. We ought not to give so little thought to a matter of such moment, or let foreigners persuade us into a war with which we have nothing to do. And yet, as an individual, I gain in honor by such a course, and I fear for my person as little as other men do. I do not think a man is any the worse citizen for taking some thought for his person and estate; on the contrary, such a man would, for his own sake, desire his country’s prosperity more than others. Nevertheless, as I have never spoken against my convictions to gain honor, I shall not begin now, but shall say what I think best. Any words of mine would be weak against your character, if I were to advise you to keep what you have got and not to risk what is actually yours for advantages that are dubious in themselves and that you may or may not attain. I will therefore content myself with showing that your ardor is out of season, and that your ambition is not easy to accomplish.

“I affirm, then, that in going there you leave many enemies behind you here, and bring more back with you. Perhaps you imagine that the treaty you have made can be trusted. So long as you keep quiet it will go on existing in name (for in name only it has become, through the practices of certain men here and at Sparta). But if you suffered a serious reverse anywhere, our enemies would not hesitate a moment to attack us. The reason is, first, that disaster forced the convention on them and it brought them less honor than it brought us; and second, that the convention itself contains many points still in dispute. Again, some of the most powerful states have never accepted the arrangement at all. Some of them are at open war with us. Others are held back only by truces renewed every ten days, since the Lacedaemonians have not yet moved. And it is only too probable that if they saw our power divided, as we are hurrying to divide it, they would attack us with vigor, together with the Siceliots, whose alliance they would once have valued as they would that of few others. A man ought therefore to weigh these points. He ought not to think of gambling with a country in so critical a position, or of reaching for another empire before we have made the one we hold secure. The Thracian Chalcidians, after all, have been in revolt from us all these years and are still not subdued, and others on the continents obey us only doubtfully. Meanwhile our allies the Egestaeans have been wronged, and we hurry to their help, while the rebels who have wronged us for so long are still waiting for their punishment.

“And yet the rebels, if we brought them under, we could keep under. The Sicilians, even if we conquered them, are too far off and too numerous to be ruled without difficulty. It is folly to attack men whom we could not hold even after conquering them, when failure would leave us in a very different position from the one we occupied before the enterprise began. Consider the Siceliots as they are at present. Suppose the Syracusans conquered them (the favorite bugbear of the Egestaeans). To my thinking they would then be even less dangerous to us than before. As things stand, they might possibly come against us here as separate states, out of love for Lacedaemon. In the other case one empire would hardly attack another. If they joined the Peloponnesians to overthrow ours, they could expect only to see the same hands overthrow their own in the same way. The Hellenes in Sicily would fear us most if we never went there at all, and next, if we showed our power and then left again as soon as possible. We all know that what is farthest away, and what has the reputation least open to test, is what men admire. At the first reverse they would begin to look down on us, and would join our enemies here against us. You have yourselves had this experience with the Lacedaemonians and their allies. Your success against them was unexpected, compared with what you feared at first, and it has made you suddenly despise them; it tempts you further to aim at the conquest of Sicily. You ought not to be puffed up by your adversaries’ misfortunes. You ought to think of breaking their spirit before you give yourselves up to confidence. And you ought to understand that their disgrace has put one thought into the Lacedaemonians: how they may still, if possible, overthrow us and repair their dishonor, since military reputation is their oldest and chief study. Our struggle, therefore, if we are wise, will not be for the barbarian Egestaeans in Sicily, but for the best defense of ourselves against the oligarchical machinations of Lacedaemon.

“We should also remember that only now are we getting some respite from a great plague and from war, to the no small benefit of our estates and persons. It is right to spend these resources at home, for ourselves, and not for these exiles. It is in the exiles’ interest to lie as plausibly as they can. They contribute nothing but talk and leave the danger to others; if they succeed they will show no proper gratitude, and if they fail they will drag their friends down with them. Suppose, too, that some man here is overjoyed at being chosen to command and urges you to make the expedition merely for his own ends, particularly if he is still too young to command. He wants to be admired for his stud of horses, and since it is so expensive, hopes to make some profit from his appointment. Do not allow such a man to keep up his private splendor at his country’s risk. Remember that such persons damage the public fortune while they squander their own, and that this is a matter of importance, not one for a young man to decide or hastily to take in hand.

“When I see such persons sitting here beside that same individual, summoned by him, alarm seizes me. I in my turn call on any older man who has such a person sitting next to him not to let himself be shamed out of his opinion, for fear of being thought a coward if he does not vote for war. Let him remember that success rarely comes from wishing and often from forecast. Let him leave the mad dream of conquest to them, and as a true lover of his country, now threatened by the greatest danger in its history, raise his hand on the other side. Let him vote that the Siceliots keep the limits now existing between us, limits no one can complain of (the Ionian sea for the coasting voyage, and the Sicilian sea across the open main), and enjoy their own possessions and settle their own quarrels. Let him vote that the Egestaeans be told to end by themselves, with the Selinuntines, the war they began without consulting the Athenians. And let him vote that in future we make no more alliances, as we have been accustomed to do, with people we must help in their need and who can never help us in ours.

“And you, Prytanis, if you think it your duty to care for the commonwealth, and want to show yourself a good citizen, put the question to the vote and ask the Athenians for their opinions a second time. If you fear to move the question again, consider that a violation of the law cannot bring blame on you when so many share in it. You will be the physician of your misguided city. The virtue of men in office is simply this: to do their country as much good as they can, or at least as little harm as they can avoid.”

Such were the words of Nicias. Most of the Athenians who came forward spoke in favor of the expedition and of not annulling what had been voted, although some spoke on the other side. By far the warmest advocate of the expedition, however, was Alcibiades, son of Clinias. He wished to thwart Nicias, who was his political opponent and had also attacked him in his speech; and he was besides exceedingly ambitious for a command by which he hoped to reduce Sicily and Carthage, and to gain wealth and reputation personally by his successes. The position he held among the citizens led him to indulge his tastes beyond what his real means could bear, both in keeping horses and in the rest of his expenditure; and this later had not a little to do with the ruin of the Athenian state. The mass of the people were alarmed at the greatness of his license in his own life and habits, and at the ambition he showed in everything he undertook. They set him down as a pretender to the tyranny, and became his enemies. Publicly his conduct of the war was as good as could be desired, but individually his habits gave offense to everyone, and so they committed affairs to other hands, and before long ruined the city. Meanwhile he now came forward and gave the Athenians the following advice:

“Athenians, I have a better right to command than others (I must start with this, since Nicias has attacked me), and I believe I am worthy of it. What I am abused for brings fame to my ancestors and to me, and profit to the country as well. The Hellenes had expected our city to be ruined by the war. They came to think it even greater than it really is, because of the magnificence with which I represented it at the Olympic games. I entered seven chariots, more than any private person had ever entered, and took first prize, and second and fourth, and saw that everything else was done in a style worthy of my victory. Custom counts such displays honorable, and they always leave behind an impression of power. Again, whatever splendor I have shown at home, by furnishing choruses or in other ways, naturally draws envy from my fellow citizens, but to foreigners it looks like strength, just as the other did. And this is no useless folly, when a man at his own cost benefits his city as well as himself. Nor is it unfair that a man proud of his position should refuse to stand on an equality with the rest. The man who is badly off bears his misfortunes alone, and as nobody courts a man in adversity, on the same principle one ought to put up with the insolence of the prosperous. Otherwise let him first treat all men equally, and then demand equal treatment himself. This much I know: such persons, and all others who have reached any distinction, may be unpopular in their lifetime with their fellow men, and especially with their equals. But they leave behind them a desire among posterity to claim kinship with them even with no grounds, and the country they belonged to boasts of them, not as strangers or wrongdoers, but as fellow countrymen and heroes. These are my aspirations, and however I am abused for them in private, the question is whether anyone handles public affairs better than I do. I united the most powerful states of Peloponnese, without great danger or expense to you, and forced the Lacedaemonians to stake everything on one day’s fighting at Mantinea. They won the battle, but they have never fully recovered their confidence since.

“So my youth and my so-called monstrous folly found fitting arguments to meet the power of the Peloponnesians, and by their ardor won the Peloponnesians’ confidence and prevailed. Do not be afraid of my youth now. While I am still in its flower, and Nicias seems fortunate, make the fullest use of both of us. Do not rescind your resolution to sail to Sicily on the ground that you would be attacking a great power. The cities in Sicily are filled with a motley rabble and readily change their institutions and take up new ones. As a result their inhabitants have no feeling of patriotism, are not armed for their own defense, and have not properly settled on the land. Each man thinks he can get something out of the public purse by fair words or by party strife, and that if disaster comes he can settle in some other country; so he makes his preparations accordingly. From such a mob you need not expect unanimity in counsel or concert in action. They will probably come over one by one as they are offered fair terms, especially if they are torn by civil strife, as we are told. Moreover, the Siceliots do not have as many heavy infantry as they boast. The Hellenes generally proved less numerous than each state reckoned itself, and Hellas greatly overestimated their numbers and has scarcely had an adequate force of heavy infantry at any time in this war; the same will be true here. From all that I hear, then, the states in Sicily will be found to be as I say. And I have not listed all our advantages, for we shall have the help of many barbarians, who hate the Syracusans and will join us in attacking them. Nor will the powers at home prove any hindrance, if you judge rightly. Our fathers won the empire resting only on their superiority at sea, against these very adversaries, whom we are told we shall leave behind us when we sail, and with the Mede as their enemy as well. The Peloponnesians have never had so little hope against us as now. However sanguine they are, and though they are strong enough to invade our country even if we stay at home, they can never hurt us with their navy, since we leave one of our own behind us that is a match for them.

“In this state of things, what reason can we give ourselves for holding back, or what excuse can we make to our allies in Sicily for not helping them? They are our confederates, and we are bound to assist them; we cannot object that they have not assisted us. We did not take them into alliance so that they would help us in Hellas, but so that they would harass our enemies in Sicily and keep them from crossing over here to attack us. That is how empire has been won, by us and by everyone else who has held one: by a constant readiness to support anyone who asks for help, whether barbarian or Hellene. If all were to keep quiet, or to pick and choose whom they should assist, we should make very few new conquests and should put in danger those we have already won. Men are not content with warding off the attacks of a superior; they often strike the first blow to prevent the attack from coming. And we cannot decide at what exact point our empire is to stop. We have reached a position where we must not be content with keeping it, but must plan to extend it; for if we stop ruling others, we are in danger of being ruled ourselves. Nor can you look at inaction in the same way as others do, unless you are ready to change your habits and make them like theirs.”

“Be convinced, then, that this adventure abroad will increase our power at home. Let us make the expedition and humble the pride of the Peloponnesians. Let us sail off to Sicily and show them how little we care for the peace we are now enjoying. At the same time we shall either become masters of the whole of Hellas, as we very easily may, through the accession of the Sicilian Hellenes, or at any rate ruin the Syracusans, to the no small advantage of ourselves and our allies. Our navy will secure our freedom to stay if we succeed or to return, for we shall be superior at sea to all the Siceliots put together. Do not let Nicias turn you from your purpose, with the do-nothing policy he advocates and his setting of the young against the old. Follow the good old fashion by which our fathers, old and young together, brought our affairs to their present height by their united counsels, and endeavor still to advance them. Understand that neither youth nor old age can do anything without the other, and that levity, sobriety and deliberate judgment are strongest when united. Understand too that if the city sinks into inaction, it will wear itself out like everything else, and its skill in everything will decay, while each fresh struggle will give it fresh experience and make it more used to defending itself not in word but in deed. In short, my conviction is that a city not inactive by nature could choose no quicker way to ruin itself than by suddenly adopting such a policy. The safest rule of life is to take one’s character and institutions for better and for worse, and to live up to them as closely as one can.”

Such were the words of Alcibiades. The Athenians heard him, and then the Egestaeans and some Leontine exiles, who came forward to remind them of their oaths and to implore their assistance. They became more eager for the expedition than before. Nicias saw that it was now useless to try to deter them by the old line of argument. He thought, however, that he might perhaps change their resolution by the extravagance of his estimates, and so he came forward a second time and spoke as follows:

“I see, Athenians, that you are thoroughly set on the expedition. I hope, then, that everything turns out as we wish, and I will now give you my opinion on where we stand. By all I hear, the cities we are marching against are great, and they are not subject to one another. They feel no need of change that would make them glad to exchange forced servitude for an easier condition, and they are not in the least likely to take our rule in place of freedom. Counting only the Hellenic towns, they are very numerous for a single island. Naxos and Catana, which I expect to join us because of their tie with Leontini, are two. Beyond them there are seven others, armed at every point just as our own power is, and above all Selinus and Syracuse, the chief objects of our expedition. These cities are full of heavy infantry, archers and darters. Galleys they have in abundance, and crowds to man them. They have money too: some in private hands, some in the temples at Selinus, and at Syracuse first-fruits from certain barbarians as well. Their chief advantage over us, however, is their number of horses, and the fact that they grow their own corn instead of importing it.

“Against a power of this kind we shall need more than a weak naval armament. We shall want a large land army to sail with us as well, if we are to achieve anything worthy of our ambition and are not to be shut out of the country by their numerous cavalry. That is especially so if the cities take alarm and combine, and we are left with no friends (except the Egestaeans) to provide us with horse to defend ourselves. To retire under compulsion, or to send back for reinforcements because we did not think the matter through at the start, would be disgraceful. We must therefore set out from home with a competent force, since we are going to sail far from our country on an expedition unlike any you have undertaken among your subject states here in Hellas, where any additional supplies needed were easily drawn from friendly territory. We, however, are cutting ourselves off and going to a land entirely strange, from which for four months in winter a messenger can hardly even get through to Athens.

“I think, therefore, that we ought to take great numbers of heavy infantry, both from Athens and from our allies. We should take not merely those of our subjects, but also any we can get for love or for money in Peloponnese. We need great numbers also of archers and slingers, to make head against the Sicilian horse. Meanwhile we must have an overwhelming superiority at sea, so that we can more easily carry in what we want. We must take our own corn in merchant vessels, that is to say wheat and parched barley, and bakers from the mills, compelled to serve for pay in the proper proportion. In this way, if we are weather-bound, the armament will not want provisions, since not every city will be able to entertain numbers like ours. We must also provide ourselves with everything else as far as we can, so as not to depend on others. Above all, we must take with us from home as much money as possible, for the sums talked of as ready at Egesta are readier, you may be sure, in talk than in any other way.

“Indeed, suppose we leave Athens with a force that matches the enemy’s, except in the number of heavy infantry he can put in the field, or even one that is superior to him at every point. We shall still find it hard to conquer Sicily or to save ourselves. We must not hide from ourselves that we are going to found a city among strangers and enemies. A man who undertakes such an enterprise must be ready to become master of the country on the very day he lands, or else to find everything hostile to him if he fails. I fear this. I know that we shall need much good counsel and still more good fortune — a hard thing for a mortal man to hope for. So before sailing I wish, as far as I can, to make myself independent of fortune, and when I do sail, to be as safe as a strong force can make me. This I believe to be surest for the country at large and safest for those of us who are to go on the expedition. If anyone thinks otherwise, I give up my command to him.”

With this Nicias concluded. He thought that he would either disgust the Athenians by the magnitude of the undertaking or, if he was obliged to sail on the expedition, would at least sail in the safest way possible. The Athenians, however, were far from having their taste for the voyage taken away by the burden of the preparations. They became more eager for it than ever, and the very opposite of what Nicias had expected took place. They held that he had given good advice, and that the expedition would now be the safest in the world. All alike fell in love with the enterprise. The older men thought that they would either subdue the places against which they were to sail or, with so large a force, at all events meet with no disaster. Those in the prime of life felt a longing for foreign sights and spectacles, and had no doubt that they would come safe home again. The common people and the soldiery thought of earning wages at the moment, and of making conquests that would supply a never-ending fund of pay for the future. The enthusiasm of the majority was such that the few who disliked the plan feared to appear unpatriotic by holding up their hands against it, and so kept quiet.

At last one of the Athenians came forward and called upon Nicias. He told him that he ought not to make excuses or put them off, but to say at once, before them all, what forces the Athenians should vote him. Nicias said, not without reluctance, that he would rather consider that matter at leisure with his colleagues. As far as he could see at present, however, they must sail with at least one hundred galleys. The Athenians would provide as many transports as they decided on, and would send for others from the allies. They must take not less than five thousand heavy infantry in all, Athenian and allied, and more if possible, and the rest of the armament in proportion. Archers from home and from Crete, slingers, and whatever else seemed desirable would be got ready by the generals and taken with them.

When the Athenians heard this, they voted at once that the generals should have full powers over the size of the army and over the whole expedition, to act as they judged best for the interests of Athens. The preparations then began. Messages went out to the allies, and the rolls were drawn up at home. Everything was provided the more easily because the city had just recovered from the plague and the long war, because a generation of young men had grown up, and because the truce had allowed capital to accumulate.

While these preparations were going on, most of the stone Hermae in the city of Athens had their faces mutilated in a single night. These are the familiar square figures that stand so commonly in the doorways of private houses and temples. No one knew the culprits, but large public rewards were offered for finding them. A further vote invited anyone who knew of any other act of impiety to come forward and give information without fear of consequences, whether he were citizen, alien or slave. The matter was taken up the more seriously because it was held to be an omen for the expedition, and part of a conspiracy to start a revolution and to overthrow the democracy.

Some resident aliens and body servants then came forward with information. It concerned not the Hermae but earlier mutilations of other images, committed by young men in a drunken frolic, and mock celebrations of the mysteries, said to be held in private houses. Alcibiades was implicated in this charge. The men who seized on it were those who could least endure him, since he stood in the way of their gaining undisturbed leadership of the people, and who believed that the first place would be theirs once he was removed. They made much of the matter and loudly declared that the mysteries and the mutilation of the Hermae were both part of a scheme to overthrow the democracy, and that nothing of it had been done without Alcibiades. As proof they pointed to the general and undemocratic license of his life and habits.

Alcibiades answered the charges on the spot. Before sailing, now that the preparations were complete, he also offered to stand trial, so that it could be seen whether he was guilty of what was charged against him. If found guilty, he wished to be punished. If acquitted, he wished to take the command. In the meantime he protested against their listening to slanders about him in his absence. He begged them to put him to death at once if he were guilty, and he pointed out how imprudent it was to send him at the head of so large an army while so serious a charge remained undecided. But his enemies feared that the army would be for him if he were tried immediately, and that the people might soften toward a man they already courted as the reason the Argives and some of the Mantineans were joining the expedition. They did all they could to defeat his proposal. They put up other orators who said that he should sail for now and not hold up the army’s departure, and that he should be tried on his return within a set number of days. Their plan was to have him sent for and brought home to face some graver charge, which they could more easily contrive in his absence. So it was decreed that he should sail.

After this the departure for Sicily took place, at about midsummer. Most of the allies, with the corn transports, the smaller craft and the rest of the expedition, had already been ordered to gather at Corcyra, so as to cross the Ionian Sea from there together to the Iapygian promontory. The Athenians themselves, with those of their allies who happened to be present, went down to Piraeus on the appointed day at daybreak and began to man the ships to put out to sea. The whole population of the city, one may say, went down with them, citizens and foreigners alike. The people of the country each escorted their own, whether friends, relatives or sons, with hope and with lamentation as they went. They thought of the conquests they hoped to make, or of the friends they might never see again, given the long voyage ahead of them, away from their country. At this moment, as they were about to part, the danger came home to them more than when they voted for the expedition. Even so, the strength of the armament and the lavish provision they saw in every department could not but comfort them. The foreigners and the rest of the crowd simply came to see a sight worth seeing and beyond belief.

This first armament to sail out was by far the most costly and splendid Hellenic force ever sent out by a single city up to that time. In mere numbers of ships and heavy infantry, the force sent against Epidaurus under Pericles, and the same force when it went against Potidæa under Hagnon, was its equal. That force had four thousand Athenian heavy infantry, three hundred horse and one hundred galleys, with fifty Lesbian and Chian vessels and many allies besides. But those forces went on a short voyage and with scanty equipment. The present expedition was planned for a long term of service by land and sea alike, and ships and troops were supplied so that it would be ready for either as required. The fleet was fitted out with great care, at great cost to the captains and the state. The treasury paid each seaman a drachma a day and supplied the empty ships, sixty warships and forty transports, which it manned with the best crews obtainable. The captains added a bounty to the treasury’s pay for the thranitae and the crews generally. They also spent lavishly on figure-heads and equipment, and every one of them strained to make his own ship outdo the rest in beauty and speed. The land forces, meanwhile, had been chosen from the best muster-rolls, and each competed with the others in the care they gave to their arms and personal accoutrements. The result was a rivalry among themselves in their separate departments, and an impression among the rest of the Hellenes that this was more a display of power and resources than an armament against an enemy. Suppose someone had added up the public expenditure of the state and the private outlay of individuals. On the public side he would count what the state had already spent on the expedition and what it was sending out in the generals’ hands. On the private side he would count what individuals had spent on their personal outfit, and what captains of galleys had laid out, and were still to lay out, on their vessels. Suppose he had added the journey money that each man was likely to have provided for himself, apart from the treasury’s pay, for so long a voyage, and what soldiers or traders took with them to exchange. He would have found that many talents in all were being taken out of the city. The expedition became just as famous for its astonishing boldness and the splendor of its appearance as for its overwhelming strength compared with the peoples it was aimed at. It was famous too because this was the longest passage from home yet attempted, and the most ambitious in its objects given the resources of those who undertook it.

The ships were now manned, and everything they meant to sail with had been put on board. The trumpet commanded silence, and the prayers customary before putting out to sea were offered, not in each ship by itself, but by all together, following the voice of a herald. Bowls of wine were mixed throughout the armament, and the soldiers and their officers made libations in gold and silver goblets. The crowds on shore, the citizens and all others who wished them well, joined in their prayers. The hymn was sung and the libations finished, and then they put out to sea. At first they sailed out in column, then raced each other as far as Aegina, and so hastened to reach Corcyra, where the rest of the allied forces were also assembling.
